analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on long-term investment gains to 15% and lets sellers subtract inflation from their taxable gains.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: it was referred there on the day it was introduced in July 1989 and died when the Congress ended, with no committee vote and no floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the top tax rate on long-term capital gains — the profit from selling stocks, businesses, or other assets held more than a year — from 34% down to 15%, for both individuals and corporations. It also would have allowed sellers of corporate stock and business property to inflate their cost basis for inflation, so price increases caused by inflation would no longer be taxed as profit. The rate cut would have applied to sales after 1989 and included a safety valve: the lower rate would expire if capital-gains tax revenue in 1995 failed to exceed 1989 levels.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and corporations that sell capital assets, a benefit concentrated among the wealthiest households, since capital gains income flows heavily to high earners. Shareholders and holders of business property would pay at most 15 cents per dollar of long-term gain instead of up to 34 cents, and indexing would erase tax on gains that merely match inflation.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the tax rate on an individual's net long-term capital gain at 15%, down from the up-to-34% rate then in effect, and applies the same 15% ceiling to corporate capital gains [S2][S3].

Indexes the cost basis of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year to the gross national product deflator, so gains attributable to inflation are not taxed at all; the indexing provision would take effect for sales after 1994 [S2][S3].
Reduces the minimum-tax rate applied to capital gains to 15%, extending the lower rate to taxpayers otherwise subject to the alternative minimum tax [S3].
Includes a built-in test: the 15% rate would terminate if Treasury data showed capital-gains tax revenue in 1995 had not exceeded 1989 revenue, a designed check on the revenue cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, would absorb the lost revenue; the benefit of lower rates and inflation indexing goes overwhelmingly to households and companies with large capital gains, so the tax burden would shift toward income from work.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is highly concentrated: most capital gains are reported by high-income households, so a 15% ceiling and inflation indexing would deliver most of its value to the top of the income distribution while reducing federal revenue available for other purposes [S2].

Indexing would permanently remove from taxation any gain that merely keeps pace with inflation, shrinking the tax base for one of the few taxes whose burden falls mainly on wealth rather than wages [S2][S3].

Even supporters would have had to acknowledge the revenue risk: the bill itself contained a provision to repeal the 15% rate if capital-gains revenue in 1995 did not exceed 1989 levels, an admission the cut might not pay for itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a large, targeted tax cut to investors and corporations, with the strongest argument for it being a simpler, lower rate that discourages holding assets just to avoid tax. Against that, the cost would fall on the federal budget while nearly all of the benefit flows to the wealthiest households, and the bill's own sunset test acknowledged the revenue might never materialize. The inflation-indexing piece has a respectable economic logic, but attaching it to a steep rate cut weighted the bill heavily toward those with large portfolios.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up, so the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Kasten introduced S. 1286 on July 11, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
The bill received a single cosponsor, a Republican colleague in the 45-member Senate Republican conference [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and no floor vote was ever scheduled before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill mainly would have cut taxes on investment gains concentrated among the wealthy, its quiet death preserved existing capital-gains rates and the revenue they raised. Federal coffers and wage-earning taxpayers were better off than under the bill; investors seeking the 15% rate gained nothing.

for.name: 1 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never reported it out, held no markup, and took no recorded action on it.

against.name: Senate majority
against.role: Senate leadership that controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action there was nothing to schedule.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican and its only cosponsor was a Republican; it never advanced far enough for a floor vote where party lines could be measured, but the Democratic majority that controlled the Finance Committee and the floor took no action on it.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of corporate stock and business assets
industries.note: The bill would have capped their tax on long-term gains at 15% and indexed their cost basis for inflation, benefits that flow almost entirely to high-income households; the offset is forgone federal revenue that other taxpayers ultimately cover.
Corporate capital gains would have been taxed at 15% instead of the 34% corporate rate, directly reducing tax on corporate asset sales at public revenue's expense.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill included pass-through rules letting regulated investment companies, REITs, and common trust funds pass inflation-indexed basis to their shareholders, extending the benefit to fund and REIT investors.
